newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia says infotech pact unlikely at Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says infotech pact unlikely at Singapore.

text.p: Malaysia said on Tuesday it is opposed to negotiating the elimination of tariffs on information technology at the World Trade Organisation's meeting here and did not see a pact being reached on the subject in Singapore.
"We did not come here to discuss the Information Technology Agreement (ITA)," international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz told reporters. "All negotiations should be done in Geneva."

European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said earlier that the EU, the United States, Canada and Japan were making progress in solving differences over a global ITA pact and hoped to continue progress in talks later in the day.

Rafidah said if three or four countries came together with a deal on the ITA, Malaysia would not be a party to it. "And I've checked with my friends in ASEAN, we did not come here to negotiate, so there is no question of acceding to anything."
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations groups Malaysia with Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam.

Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista also said earlier on Tuesday that there was little chance of a concrete agreement being reached in Singapore to eliminate information technology tariffs.
Rafidah said Malaysia was not afraid of being left out if developed countries reached accord.
"We come in when we are ready. Let's go to Geneva and have the right format for that...we need the flexibility to discuss the right time frame, product coverage and the rest."
She added that Malaysia was prepared to study a draft agreement and leave it to be negotiated at the WTO's headquarters in Geneva.

Rafidah said earlier that the Group of 15 (G15) developing nations had also discussed the ITA, which could scrap an estimated $600 billion worth of annual exports globally in computer and telecommunication products.
She said Malaysia supports an ITA, but one that would offer countries the flexibility of going beyond a year 2000 target in making tariff cuts.
Rafidah also predicted there would be no new trade liberalisation steps agreed at the Singapore ministerial meeting.

"In the Singapore meeting we can't achieve extra liberalisation. We are not here to negotiate market access or anything of that sort. We are here to review what we have done so far and all these discussions on these issues are extraneous."
